claims.statement: Alcibiades was an Athenian politician and commander whose career crossed the divisions of the Peloponnesian War. Brought up under Pericles’ guardianship, he became closely associated with Socrates. He helped persuade Athens to send its great expedition to Sicily, then fled to Sparta after being recalled for trial. His later return to Athenian service makes his life a useful way through the war’s changing alliances.

His later return to Athenian service makes his life a useful way through the war’s changing alliances.

claims.statement: Pericles was an Athenian politician and commander, born around 495 BCE. His career belonged to the period when Athens became a dominant power in the Greek world. He was still leading the city at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the epidemic in 429 BCE, early in a conflict that would continue for another quarter of a century.

value.text: Pericles was an Athenian politician and commander, born around 495 BCE. His career belonged to the period when Athens became a dominant power in the Greek world. He was still leading the city at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the epidemic in 429 BCE, early in a conflict that would continue for another quarter of a century.

claims.statement: Nicias was an Athenian commander and politician who favoured peace with Sparta. The treaty negotiated in 421 BCE bears his name. He opposed the proposed expedition to Sicily but nevertheless became one of its commanders alongside Alcibiades and Lamachus. His career ended with the expedition’s defeat in 413 BCE.

claims.statement: Sparta led the coalition fighting Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Its victory in 404 BCE forced Athens to give up its empire. Alcibiades’ connection takes you inside that rivalry: after leaving Athenian service, he sought refuge with the Spartans and advised them against his own city.

Syracuse was the principal target of the Athenian expedition to Sicily. Its defenders, aided by the Spartan commander Gylippus, resisted the siege. The Athenian expedition was destroyed in 413 BCE. Syracuse’s connections show this part of the war from the city being attacked, rather than only from Athens.

The Peloponnesian War set Athens and its allies against Sparta and its coalition. It ran from 431 to 404 BCE, with a negotiated peace interrupting the main conflict. Fighting extended well beyond the two cities. The Sicilian expedition and Persian involvement are part of the same history. Athens eventually surrendered and lost its empire.

claims.statement: A severe epidemic struck Athens during the early years of the war. People had crowded into the city for protection, and the disease killed soldiers and civilians, including Pericles in 429 BCE. Thucydides survived it and described what he saw. The illness is conventionally called the plague of Athens, but its precise cause remains uncertain.

Socrates and Alcibiades were deployed to Potidaea in 432 BCE. Socrates served as a hoplite, an infantry soldier. The episode places their relationship in military service as well as philosophical conversation.

claims.statement: Socrates fought at Delium in 424 BCE, when the Athenian army was defeated. Plato’s dialogues later present Alcibiades and Laches praising his conduct during the retreat. These are literary accounts of the event, not transcripts made on the battlefield.

claims.statement: Athens and Sparta agreed to peace in 421 BCE after ten years of war. Nicias was closely associated with the negotiations. The settlement did not resolve the rivalries between the cities and their allies. The later Sicilian expedition and renewed war show how limited the peace proved.

claims.statement: Athens sent a major expedition to Sicily in 415 BCE. Alcibiades, Nicias and Lamachus shared the initial command. Alcibiades was recalled, and the remaining commanders pursued the campaign against Syracuse. Despite reinforcements, the expedition ended in disaster in 413 BCE. Many survivors became prisoners.

Just before the fleet sailed for Sicily, sacred stone figures called herms were mutilated across Athens. The attack provoked an investigation into sacrilege. Alcibiades became caught up in accusations concerning religious offences. Accusations against him should not be read as proof that he personally damaged the herms.

Recalled from Sicily for trial in 415 BCE, Alcibiades escaped to Sparta. He advised Athens’ enemies as the war widened. By 412 BCE he was helping Spartan operations in Ionia. This was a changing political allegiance, not an uninterrupted stay in the city of Sparta.

An oligarchic coup replaced Athenian democracy with the government of the Four Hundred in 411 BCE. Hopes of obtaining Persian support formed part of the political manoeuvring. Alcibiades was involved in proposals linking a change of government to his own return. The new regime was divided from the start.

After the naval victory at Arginusae in 406 BCE, Athens prosecuted the commanders over the failure to recover men and bodies from the sea. Socrates opposed the unlawful collective proceedings. Six generals were executed.

claims.statement: Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, ending the Peloponnesian War. Its Long Walls were demolished. Peace did not immediately restore political stability. The government of the Thirty and a civil conflict followed.

After Athens’ defeat, an oligarchic government known as the Thirty took power with Spartan backing. Opposition to its rule developed into civil war. The regime was short-lived. Democratic forces recovered ground, and a settlement in 403 BCE restored democracy.

A settlement in 403 BCE restored Athenian democracy after the rule of the Thirty and the fighting that followed. The Spartan king Pausanias intervened in the reconciliation. Socrates’ trial belongs to this restored democracy, four years later. The two events should not be collapsed into one.

Darius II ruled the Persian Empire during the later years of the Peloponnesian War. His officials negotiated with Sparta, and Persian money helped support its fleet. This places the war within a wider struggle over influence in the Aegean and western Anatolia. Persia was an active participant, not just a distant background.

claims.statement: Around 404 BCE, Amyrtaeus established himself as an Egyptian ruler and began consolidating independence from Persia. He was the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty. The change did not happen everywhere at once. Documents from Elephantine still recognised the Persian king as late as 401 BCE. This is a gradual political transition, despite the single date on the timeline.
